description: Local residents expressed strong opposition to a proposed solar farm at an August 21, 2023 meeting reviewing the possible construction of a 160-MW, 1,000-acre solar panel array.
long_description: Local residents expressed strong opposition to a proposed solar farm at an August 21, 2023 meeting reviewing the possible construction of a 160-MW, 1,000-acre solar panel array. The residents opposed the farm for several reasons, including that the farm would be powering communities “over an hour away” and not their own; that the solar farm might encroach on family properties that have existed for generations; and that potential road runoff might impact their well water supplies. Residents also expressed frustration that surveyors had entered their property without their permission. An online petition created by the group “Concerned Citizens of Covington County Alabama” urged Origis Energy to relocate the project to a more remote or industrial area of Covington County. As of December 31, 2023, the petition had 80 signatures.

project_name: Stockton I and Stockton II Solar
description: In October 2025, Alabama Power submitted its proposal for two solar projects, the 80-MW Stockton I and the 180-MW Stockton II, to be located on approximately 2,000 acres of land in Stockton.
long_description: In October 2025, Alabama Power submitted its proposal for two solar projects, the 80-MW Stockton I and the 180-MW Stockton II, to be located on approximately 2,000 acres of land in Stockton. The projects were designed to power a Meta-affiliated data center under construction in Montgomery. Local residents have voiced concerns about the projects, including the impacts on the community’s rural character and wetlands as well as its proximity to the Mobile-Tensaw Delta and the potential environmental risks posed by hurricanes and flooding. The opponents created a Facebook page titled “Stop Solar in Stockton,” where residents have raised concerns about land use, environmental impacts, and the lack of public notice. In December 2025, the Alabama Public Service Commission unanimously approved the projects. Construction is expected to begin in 2026, with commercial operation by the end of 2028.

description: In July 2018, American Electric Power abandoned plans to build a $4.5 billion, 2,000-MW wind farm in the Oklahoma panhandle, as well as an associated interstate transmission project that would have delivered electricity to Arkansas and other states.
long_description: In July 2018, American Electric Power abandoned plans to build a $4.5 billion, 2,000-MW wind farm in the Oklahoma panhandle, as well as an associated interstate transmission project that would have delivered electricity to Arkansas and other states. In Arkansas, a dark money group called Protect Our Pocketbooks paid for television advertisements claiming that Arkansas would receive no benefits from the project. The developer responded by issuing a statement that Protect Our Pocketbooks was “presenting misleading information to the public, including manipulation of statements by Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson.” The developer further noted that the group “does not reveal the names of its backers or the sources of its substantial funding.” Although the Arkansas Public Service Commission ultimately granted approval for the Arkansas components of the project, the Wind Catcher project was canceled altogether when the Texas Public Service Commission (PSC) denied approval.

long_description: The developer Nature and People First has sought to develop a 6,000-MW, utility-scale pumped storage hydropower project on approximately 400 acres of land. In July 2023, three organizations—Tó Nizhóní Ání, Diné Citizens Against Ruining our Environment, and Center for Biological Diversity—submitted a letter to FERC attaching resolutions against the project from 18 Navajo Nation chapters and agencies. Nearby residents had expressed concerns that the project could damage underground water supplies and sacred lands and that the developer had not sufficiently involved nearby residents. In February 2024, FERC denied applications for a preliminary permit for the project, stating that “[t]he Commission will not issue preliminary permits for projects proposing to use Tribal lands if the Tribes on whose land the project is to be located opposes the permit.”

description: In 2025, Repsol proposed the 450 MW Lava Solar Project to be located on approximately 3,700 acres of public lands in Apache County.
long_description: In 2025, Repsol proposed the 450 MW Lava Solar Project to be located on approximately 3,700 acres of public lands in Apache County. The developer has also proposed to construct a 27-mile transmission line that would serve the Lava Run Wind and the Lava Run Solar projects. The project has faced strong opposition from a group called “Stop Lava Run” that was formed with the sole purpose of opposing the Lava Run Solar and Lava Run Wind projects. The group maintains a website encouraging local residents to file public comments in opposition to the project and attend public hearings to raise concerns, including the project’s potential impacts on wildlife and ecosystems, water pollution as well as impacts on hunting, recreation, and tourism. In September 2025, the developer submitted an application for a Certificate of Environmental Compatibility (CEC) to the Arizona Power Plant and Transmission Line Siting Committee (LSC). In October 2025, the LSC, in an 8-2 vote, recommended approval of the CEC. In December 2025, the Arizona Corporate Commission unanimously voted to send the application back to the LSC to more fully address the concerns raised by local residents in opposition to the project.

description: In 2025, Arevia Power proposed the Silver King Energy Center, a hybrid facility with 800 MW of solar energy generation and 400 MW of thermal energy generation, to be located on approximately 8,122 acres of public lands north of Florence and east of San Tan Valley.
long_description: In 2025, Arevia Power proposed the Silver King Energy Center, a hybrid facility with 800 MW of solar energy generation and 400 MW of thermal energy generation, to be located on approximately 8,122 acres of public lands north of Florence and east of San Tan Valley. On January 15, 2026, the County Planning and Zoning Commission, in a 4-3 vote, recommended denial of three rezoning applications that would have allowed the project to move forward. On February 18, 2026, the County Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to reject the project rezoning applications. Opponents of the project expressed concerns about the visual impacts of solar panels on the desert landscape, the potential safety implications of locating a large utility-scale facility adjacent to the towns, and the impacts on the future of freeway construction. Supporters of the project noted the project benefits including significant job opportunities during construction, long-term operational jobs, and the substantial tax revenue for Pinal County and for public education, primarily lease payment revenue for the Arizona State University.

description: The SunZia transmission line is designed to transmit more than 3,600 MW of electricity generated at wind farms in New Mexico.
long_description: The SunZia transmission line is designed to transmit more than 3,600 MW of electricity generated at wind farms in New Mexico. Its routing in the San Pedro Valley prompted controversy, with the Tohono O’odham, Hopi, Zuni, and San Carlos Apache tribes claiming that the Bureau of Land Management ignored over 15 years of attempts by the tribes to recognize the valley as a culturally significant area. In January 2024, the Tohono O’odham Nation, San Carlos Apache Tribe, Center for Biological Diversity, and Archeology Southwest filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona, claiming that the review of the project violated the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). The lawsuit was dismissed in June 2024 and subsequently appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals. In May 2025, the Court of Appeals reversed the district court’s dismissal and remanded the case for further proceedings.  In April 2026, the developer, Pattern Energy, began testing the project as it nears completion. The lawsuit challenging the project remains pending in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

long_description: Opponents of two North Livermore Valley solar projects, Aramis (410 acres) and Sunwalker (70 acres), led by a group called Save North Livermore Valley, argued that the proposed locations of the projects impinge on agriculture, natural wildlife habitat, open space, and visual and scenic resources. In October 2020, two candidates running for election to the Alameda County Board of Supervisors issued a joint statement urging the board to place a moratorium on solar development on agricultural land. After the East County Board of Zoning Adjustments approved both projects, local groups stated appealed both decisions. By December 2020, three local organizations had filed appeals challenging the approval of the Aramis project. In May 2022, the Alameda County Superior Court upheld the county’s approval of the Aramis project, dismissing a lawsuit by project opponents. In July 2023, Save North Livermore Valley appealed the Superior Court’s decision. California’s First District Court of Appeals denied the appeal in August 2023.

long_description: The Boulder Brush Project is a 320-acre substation and transmission line proposed by Terra-Gen, which would connect to the 60-turbine Campo Wind Project planned for the Campo Indian Reservation. The lawsuit contended that the County’s environmental review of the project did not fully analyze the risks to wildlife and groundwater and the effects of noise disruptions. Dozens of attendees spoke in opposition and raised concerns about the project’s impact on the region’s native oak tree forests, grasslands, and wetlands. The developer estimated that the project would generate approximately $76 million in tax revenue over the next 20 years and made conservation commitments including at least 1,150 acres of oak woodland, riparian habitat and wildlife corridors.

description: In December 2025, E-Group PS proposed the 50-MW E-Group Solar project to be located on 477 acres of land in the City of Twentynine Palms.
long_description: In December 2025, E-Group PS proposed the 50-MW E-Group Solar project to be located on 477 acres of land in the City of Twentynine Palms. The City enacted a ban on commercial solar facilities, which was preempted by Assembly Bill 205 (AB 205), a state law that went into effect in June 2022. AB 205 allows the developer of a solar project at least 50 MW or more to seek approval from the California Energy Commission (CEC) and bypass any local approval process. The developer opted to seek approval from the City. At a public meeting on February 17, 2026, the City of Twentynine Palms’ Planning Commission considered adopting a resolution recommending the City Council approve a number of amendments to the General and Development Plans to establish the renewable energy land use designation that would allow the construction of the project. During the meeting, 18 of 22 local residents in attendance voiced opposition to the project, citing concerns about potential damage to the city’s vistas, excessive dust caused by grading, and impacts to the quality of life for residents and tourists. The Planning Commission moved to continue the discussion at a future meeting and ultimately decided to transfer its decision-making authority to the City Council. On March 23, 2026, the City Council held a public hearing and after a lengthy public comment session and discussion, it denied the project in a 3-1 vote, with one abstention.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: Hydro Green Energy proposed the Fort Ross Pumped Storage Project in September 2022, a project expected to be built about 1.5 miles northwest of the historic Fort Ross.
long_description: Hydro Green Energy proposed the Fort Ross Pumped Storage Project in September 2022, a project expected to be built about 1.5 miles northwest of the historic Fort Ross. In July 2023, California Senate Majority Leader Mike McGuire stated, “there is no chance a project of this size, with this scope, will ever get approval in such an environmentally sensitive region like the Sonoma Coast. . . . This project will not see the light of day.” Others quickly rallied in opposition to the proposal, including Richard Charter, director of the coastal coordination program for The Ocean Foundation, citing concerns about the project’s scale, impacts to the marine sanctuary, the lack of reliable power transmission in the area, and numerous indigenous archaeological sites in the area. At an August 2023 meeting planned by project advocates to answer community questions, local political and environmental leaders expressed strong opposition to the project. FERC denied Hydro Green Energy’s preliminary permit application in December 2023.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: In October 2021, the Shasta County Board of Supervisors upheld the Shasta County Planning Commission’s rejection of a permit application for the Fountain Wind Project, a 4,500-acre, 200-MW wind farm proposed by Repsol.
long_description: In October 2021, the Shasta County Board of Supervisors upheld the Shasta County Planning Commission’s rejection of a permit application for the Fountain Wind Project, a 4,500-acre, 200-MW wind farm proposed by Repsol. The project has faced significant opposition from the community and from the Pit River Tribe, whose ancestral homelands are within the project area. In denying the appeal, supervisors emphasized (a) the height and visibility of the turbines and (b) the potential that the presence of turbines could exacerbate the challenge of fighting wildfires. In June 2022, Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 205 into law, which allowed the developer to revive the application and the California Energy Commission to consider overruling the decision. In November 2023, Shasta County and the Pit River Tribe filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the Commission from approving the project. The California Attorney General moved for a change of venue, citing possible prejudice against the California Energy Commission in the County. In April 2024, a Shasta County Superior Court judge denied the request for a change of venue but ruled that a judge from another county would preside over the lawsuit. In October 2024, the litigation was stayed. In March 2025, the California Energy Commission’s staff assessment concluded that the benefits of the project did not outweigh its environmental costs. In November 2025, the Executive Director of the California Energy Commission recommended that the state reject the approval of the project. In December 2025, the California Energy Commission unanimously denied approval of the project.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: The Genesis Solar Energy Project is a 250-MW concentrated solar project developed by NextEra on 1,800 acres of land near the town of Blythe in Riverside County, California.
long_description: The Genesis Solar Energy Project is a 250-MW concentrated solar project developed by NextEra on 1,800 acres of land near the town of Blythe in Riverside County, California. In 2010, BLM briefly halted construction on a 125-acre portion of the site that the Colorado River Indian Tribe (CRIT) asserted was a historic crematorium, burial ground, and village for the Mojave Tribes. After the BLM found no conclusive evidence of habitation, human remains, or funerals, BLM allowed construction to resume. This led CRIT to sue NextEra in May 2012 in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, seeking to halt construction on the 125-acre portion. The court denied the tribe’s request for an injunction, and construction continued. Many cultural artifacts were destroyed during construction, compelling BLM to order NextEra to pay $3 million for an ethnographic study of the site and scholarship for Indigenous students.

long_description: On September 18, 2022, a local group called Friends of Livermore filed an administrative appeal to overturn Alameda County’s approval of the 12-acre, 2-MW Alameda Grant Line Solar 1 project. long_description: In December 2022, the U.S. Bureau of Ocean Energy Management auctioned off leases to develop offshore wind projects in two sites in the 207-square-mile Humboldt Wind Energy Area. description: The Humidor Storage Project, a 12-acre, 300-MW battery storage facility proposed by Hecate Grid, has faced significant pushback from residents of the unincorporated community of Acton in Los Angeles County.
long_description: The Humidor Storage Project, a 12-acre, 300-MW battery storage facility proposed by Hecate Grid, has faced significant pushback from residents of the unincorporated community of Acton in Los Angeles County. Residents have formed Save Our Rural Town and Acton Takes Action to campaign against the project and have raised concerns about the possibility of leaking chemicals, the threat of facility fires due to the area’s high risk of wildfires, and potential impacts on property values. The Acton Town Council has also opposed the development of battery storage facilities. In 2022, Los Angeles County approved the site plan for the project through an expedited ministerial process. The developer later expanded the project to 400 MW. Opponents of the project organized a petition and created a website, citing concerns about fire risk, environmental impacts, and property values. In September 2023, after an appeal of the county approval was denied, Save Our Rural Town filed a lawsuit seeking an injunction to stop the project.  In April 2024, the same advocacy group submitted comments to the California Energy Commission about the project, and the Acton Town Council submitted a request for the California Energy Commission to conduct an assessment of public safety concerns. In November 2024, Los Angeles County unanimously approved the Humidor storage project.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

long_description: In February 2024, two commercial fishing organizations filed a lawsuit in San Luis Obispo Superior Court seeking to block state agencies from issuing permits for site surveys for three proposed projects (Atlas Wind, Even Keel Wind, and Golden State Wind) in the 376-square-mile Morro Bay Wind Energy Area. description: The Mount Signal Solar Farm, also known as the Imperial Valley Solar Project, is an 800-MW solar project built by 8minutenergy in Imperial Valley.
long_description: The Mount Signal Solar Farm, also known as the Imperial Valley Solar Project, is an 800-MW solar project built by 8minutenergy in Imperial Valley. The project was built in three phases beginning in 2011. In November 2010, a three-day protest against the project occurred, which included members of Desert Survivors, Basin and Range Watch, Solar Done Right, the Quechan Tribe, Cocopah Tribe, Imperial Valley Environmental Justice Task Force, Comite Civico del Valle, Seeley Citizens United, and nearby residents. The project was temporarily paused in December 2010 by a preliminary injunction issued by a judge in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, in response to a lawsuit filed by the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Indian Reservation. The Quechan Tribe’s lawsuit raised claims under NEPA, the NHPA, and the FLPMA.

long_description: In June 2013, the Campo tribe’s General Council voted 44-34 against Invenergy’s proposed Kumeyaay II Project (or Shu’luuk Wind Project). description: In August 2023, Avantus proposed the Sienna Solar and Storage project, comprising up to 525 MW of solar energy generation and up to 525 MW of battery energy storage to be located on approximately 1,854 acres in Lucerne Valley.
long_description: In August 2023, Avantus proposed the Sienna Solar and Storage project, comprising up to 525 MW of solar energy generation and up to 525 MW of battery energy storage to be located on approximately 1,854 acres in Lucerne Valley. In October 2025, the San Bernardino County Planning Commission approved a conditional use permit for the project. Opponents of the project, including the Morongo Basin Conservation Association (MBCA), appealed the Commission’s decision to the County Board of Supervisors. The appeal alleged inconsistencies in the information submitted by the developer, including that the plans for the project as approved differ from the original proposal in terms of site location and capacity, raising concerns that the project will have a negative aesthetic impact and create excessive dust, and that the offsite impacts and decommissioning plans had not been properly addressed. On January 27, 2026, the County Board of Supervisors held a public hearing and unanimously voted to deny the appeal and uphold the Planning Commission’s approval of the project.

The project faced opposition from environmental groups including the Wilderness Society. BLM denied the permit in November 2014, citing the locations ecological, historical, recreational, and scenic importance.

long_description: According to an article published in February 2023, environmental groups, including the National Parks Conservation Association, are opposing plans for the 300-MW Soda Mountain Solar Project in the Mojave Desert, citing potential impacts to bighorn sheep, tortoises, and other wildlife. long_description: On November 20, 2019, the Santa Barbara County Planning Commission granted a conditional use permit and variance for construction of the 29-turbine, 5,887-acre Strauss Wind Energy Project. In January 2020, the Santa Barbara County Board of Supervisors denied the three appeals but added a condition mandating a setback from a home in the area. In March of the same year, the Board of Supervisors also denied an appeal of the design of the project. As of January 2024, the project was operational and producing enough energy to power 40,000 homes.

long_description: As described in a separate entry on the Aramis Solar Project, opponents of two North Livermore Valley solar projects, Aramis (410 acres) and Sunwalker (70 acres), led by a group called Save North Livermore Valley, argued that the proposed locations of the projects impinge on agriculture, natural wildlife habitat, open space, and visual and scenic resources. In October 2020, two candidates running for election to the Alameda County Board of Supervisors issued a joint statement urging the board to place a moratorium on solar development on agricultural land. After the East County Board of Zoning Adjustments approved both projects, local groups appealed those decision. In May 2021, the developer for Sunwalker withdrew its application while the appeal was pending.

long_description: In late 2019, Terra-Gen Wind applied to the Humboldt County Board of Supervisors to construct 47 wind turbines on the Monument and Bear River ridges near Scotia, enough to meet up to 56% of the county’s electricity load. The proposal was met with local opposition, including by members of the Wiyot tribe who argued that one of the ridges was a sacred prayer site of the Wiyot. The Board of Supervisors ultimately denied the application.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

long_description: In February 2022, the federal Bureau of Land Management denied the application for the Walker Ridge Wind Energy Project, which would have included up to 42 wind turbines on approximately 2,272 acres of BLM-managed public land in the Walker Ridge area of Lake County. The project was opposed by a group called the Protect Walker Ridge Alliance. In denying the application, BLM cited potential resource conflicts and the inadequacy of information submitted by the applicant to address such conflicts.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: Primergy Solar’s proposal to build a 155-MW solar project with 155 MW of battery storage on 1,900 acres in La Plata County, Colorado has encountered opposition from a local group called Stop Hesperus Solar.
long_description: Primergy Solar’s proposal to build a 155-MW solar project with 155 MW of battery storage on 1,900 acres in La Plata County, Colorado has encountered opposition from a local group called Stop Hesperus Solar. Opponents have objected to the placement of panels on agricultural land and argued that the project will cause an irreversible loss of wildlife habitat in a major migration corridor. In January 2023, the La Plata County Planning Department informed Primergy Solar that its application was incomplete, finding that the application did not include a water demand study, among other issues. The company likely will need to resubmit its application for the project.

long_description: In December 2018, Pueblo County denied Invenergy’s application to construct a 700-acre, 100-MW solar energy generation facility with 5 MW of battery storage. Local residents opposed the project due to concerns about fire risk, property value depreciation, and visual impacts.

description: In June 2022, Empire Electric Association (EEA) began construction on a 5-MW solar project in Montezuma, Colorado.
long_description: In June 2022, Empire Electric Association (EEA) began construction on a 5-MW solar project in Montezuma, Colorado. Residents fought the project, citing concerns about impacts to agricultural livelihoods and local wildlife, but they ultimately lost the battle to stop construction. Developers made certain concessions to residents, including setting the project back 50 feet from property lines, building an 8-foot-tall privacy fence around the project, and promising to plant trees when the project is finished.

long_description: On June 9, 2022, Pueblo County denied Leeward Renewable Energy’s application to construct a 150-MW solar project on 831 acres of private land near the Comanche power plant. In denying the application, county commissioners cited pushback from residents and concerns about property values. County planning and development staff had also previously recommended that the application be denied due to impacts on local residents. Residents wearing matching t-shirts with stop signs cheered the decision, asserting that the project would have impeded their views of mountains and wildlife.

description: Cypress Creek submitted an application for the Sundance Solar and Storage Project, which would include 75 MW of solar energy and 50 MW of battery energy storage, approximately 3.5 miles north of the town of Kiowa.
long_description: Cypress Creek submitted an application for the Sundance Solar and Storage Project, which would include 75 MW of solar energy and 50 MW of battery energy storage, approximately 3.5 miles north of the town of Kiowa. On April 22, 2025, the Elbert County Planning Commission voted 7-2 to deny a special use permit, citing concerns over property values and failure to meet the area’s rural design criteria. On May 14, 2025, with a vote of 2-1, the Board of County Commissioners approved the permit allowing the project to move forward. The project is expected to power approximately 15,000 homes and increase the county revenue from $16,000 to over $9.8 million over the next 40 years. Benefits of the “good neighbor commitment” by the developer include $200,000 in scholarships over the project’s lifespan and an additional $300,000 in community investments during the first three years of construction.

long_description: Over 200 San Miguel community-members gathered on May 16, 2023, to discuss a proposed 110-MW OneEnergy solar farm that would be built over roughly 600 acres of land. Many voiced opposition to the project and how it could ecologically and economically impact their community. In response to this opposition, the county passed a moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar projects) in order to update its zoning code. In September 2024, the San Miguel County Board of Commissioners unanimously adopted new zoning regulations on solar projects, ending the moratorium.

description: In 2011, a community group called FairwindCT filed a lawsuit challenging the Connecticut Siting Council’s approval of BNE Energy’s petition to construct six 1.6-MW wind turbines at two separate sites in the Town of Colebrook.
long_description: In 2011, a community group called FairwindCT filed a lawsuit challenging the Connecticut Siting Council’s approval of BNE Energy’s petition to construct six 1.6-MW wind turbines at two separate sites in the Town of Colebrook. The trial court dismissed the lawsuit, and, in 2014, after three years of litigation, the Connecticut Supreme Court upheld the dismissal. On January 9, 2020, BNE Energy submitted a request to the Connecticut Siting Council to modify the approved plan to allow installation of a different type of wind turbine. On March 4, 2020, FairwindCT submitted an objection to the proposed modification, but the Executive Director of the Council ultimately approved the modification request. On June 1, 2020, FairwindCT and abutting landowners filed a petition with the Council for a declaratory ruling to disallow the modification. On December 17, 2020, the Council issued a final decision upholding the modification request. FairwindCT and the abutting landowners appealed to the New Britain Judicial District Superior Court, which, in November 2021, ruled in their favor, vacating the Council’s approval of the requested modification.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

long_description: In August 2024, the Connecticut Siting Council unanimously rejected a plan for a 1.5-MW solar project, citing concerns over the developer’s plans to remove about 7.9 acres of trees. In September 2024, the developer filed an appeal to the decision. In the appeal, the developer claimed that the council “exceeded” its authority, arguing that, as the owner of the land, the developer could have cleared the trees without local zoning approval and then submitted the proposal to the Siting Council, which would have had “no basis” for denying it.

description: In July 2020, DESRI Holdings L.P. proposed the 120 MW Gravel Pit Solar Project on 737 acres in the Town of East Windsor.
long_description: In July 2020, DESRI Holdings L.P. proposed the 120 MW Gravel Pit Solar Project on 737 acres in the Town of East Windsor. On February 25, 2021, the Connecticut Siting Council (CSC) approved the project, which was completed in October 2024. In April 2025, the developer proposed an expansion of the project, which would add 30 MW of solar generation, increasing the project’s total capacity to 150 MW. The expansion proposal garnered strong opposition from local officials and a group called “East Windsor Citizens for Responsible Solar.” The opponents raised concerns over potential adverse impacts to the environment, loss of farmland, and threats to the town’s rural character. A petition opposing the expansion of the project, endorsed by State Senator Saud Anwar, gathered 2,223 signatures on change.org. In May 2025, the CSC voted 5-1 to reopen the application for the expansion. In March 2026, the CSC approved the expansion.

description: In July 2024, the Sussex County Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended approval of Renewable Redevelopment’s application for a conditional use permit to build a substation in Dagsboro to support US Wind’s offshore wind project.
long_description: In July 2024, the Sussex County Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended approval of Renewable Redevelopment’s application for a conditional use permit to build a substation in Dagsboro to support US Wind’s offshore wind project. The offshore wind project consists of 121 wind turbines and up to four offshore substations. In December 2024, the Sussex County Council, in a 4-1 vote, denied a conditional use permit for the Dagsboro substation citing lack of direct benefits to the residents of Sussex County among the reasons for denial. In June 2025, the state legislature enacted Senate Bill 159, which requires the permitting of an electric substation as an allowed conditional use in a heavy industrial zone under certain conditions, including to support the operation of a renewable energy project of 250 MW or more. The state law was given retroactive effect to August 3, 2023. The law overrides the council’s denial of the project. Sussex County and the Town of Fenwick Island, the municipalities involved in the US Wind project, challenged the law in the Delaware Court of Chancery. In March 2026, the Delaware Court of Chancery upheld the General Assembly’s authority to override Sussex County Council’s denial. In May 2026, the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed the decision by the Court of Chancery upholding the state law and overturning the Council’s denial of the conditional use permit for the Dagsboro substation.

long_description: Local opposition to the planned 24-MW Na Pua Makani wind project in Kahuku on the North Shore of Oahu reduced the scope of the project from 13-15 turbines to 8 turbines. In 2016, Keep the North Shore Country filed a contested case hearing petition to challenge the developer’s plan for mitigating impacts to endangered species including the Hawaiian Hoary Bat. In 2018, the Board of Land and Natural Resources accepted the developer’s plan and issued an incidental take license for the project. Keep the North Shore Country appealed that decision. In May 2019, the Circuit Court upheld the state agency’s decision to grant the license, and in February 2022, the Supreme Court of Hawaii affirmed on appeal. While this lawsuit was pending, Keep the North Shore Country filed a separate petition challenging the proximity of the turbines to schools and homes under Honolulu’s zoning ordinance, and an organization called Life of the Land filed a motion to block the project’s power purchase agreement. description: In August 2015, the Black Hawk County Board of Adjustment unanimously voted to deny a special permit and setback variance for Optimum Renewables’ proposed 3-turbine, 6-MW wind energy project.
county: Black Hawk County; Humboldt County; Fayette County
long_description: In August 2015, the Black Hawk County Board of Adjustment unanimously voted to deny a special permit and setback variance for Optimum Renewables’ proposed 3-turbine, 6-MW wind energy project. The decision effectively ended plans for the project in Black Hawk County, which would have been the county’s first wind farm. Roughly fifty project opponents attended the board’s meeting and expressed concerns about potential impacts to wildlife, livestock, property values, and human health. Optimum then sought to build the project in the neighboring Buchanan County. The project also met local opposition in Buchanan County, where residents expressed concerns about the project’s potential impacts to local livelihoods and voiced skepticism about promises made by project advocates. In August 2015, the Buchanan County Planning and Zoning Commission denied a rezoning application that would have allowed Optimum Renewables to build a wind farm in the county. The project was finally built in Fayette County in 2016. Opposition continued from Fayette residents, including the group Fairbank Citizens Against Industrial Wind Turbines Near Our City, who claimed that the project violated county zoning laws. In November 2016, an Iowa judge held that the project was illegal and void due to zoning violations, issuing an order requiring its removal. In May 2018, the Iowa Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal of the decision, effectively ending the project.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

In December 2024, the developer filed a lawsuit against the Board of Adjustment alleging that the denial was in bad faith as the project proposal was not subject to the 2024 moratorium halting the issuance of conditional use permits for wind projects that the county adopted within days of its application. The developer asserts that its permit application complies with the requirements of the 2011 ordinance regulating wind projects in the county. As of November 2025, the developer and the Emmet County Board of Supervisors were negotiating a settlement agreement to resolve the pending lawsuit and approve the conditional use permit for the project, subject to the terms and conditions in the agreement.

long_description: In August 2022, a local resident involved with Tama County Against Turbines Coalition filed a petition for declaratory judgment that the conditional use permits issued by the Tama County Board of Adjustment to Salt Creek Wind were illegal. Two months earlier, in June 2022, another member of the same group filed a lawsuit against the board for failing to vote on a moratorium on wind energy and for readopting the existing wind ordinance without following proper procedures. The June 2022 case was dismissed in October 2022. At a public meeting in December 2022, several residents urged the board to adopt a 6-month or 12-month moratorium. In April 2023, Salt Creek Wind, LLC sued Tama County Against Turbines and several of its individual members, claiming that the group had “chastised and bullied the [Board of] Supervisors [to] issue a moratorium on wind energy projects” and had “filed frivolous lawsuits . . . to frustrate . . . contracts between Salt Creek and the local landowners.” Also in April 2023, Southern Natural Resources, LLC (SNR) sued Salt Creek Wind, LLC and associated companies, alleging that the development was in violation of SNR’s exclusive development rights in the area and that the project misappropriated proprietary and trade secret information.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: In August 2022, the Page County Board of Supervisors approved the 200-MW Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm after 6 months of opposition from residents, who raised concerns about setbacks, noise, lighting, and decommissioning agreements.
long_description: In August 2022, the Page County Board of Supervisors approved the 200-MW Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm after 6 months of opposition from residents, who raised concerns about setbacks, noise, lighting, and decommissioning agreements. Just over a month after the approval, residents opposed to the project filed a lawsuit against the county and board in state court, which was later removed to federal court. In February 2023, after the developer, Invenergy, informed the Board of Supervisors that it would be removing 3 turbines from the plan, the Page County Zoning Administrator informed the developer that this was a “material change,” which rendered the application “void” and revoked the permit. The developer appealed the Zoning Administrator’s decision to the Page County Board of Adjustment. In March 2023, the Board of Adjustment upheld the revocation of the permit. A week later, the developer filed a lawsuit against the County officials in federal court challenging the revocation. In May 2024, the federal court denied the residents’ state claims which had been rendered moot at the time the permit was revoked. In November 2024, in a 2-1 vote, the Board of Supervisors approved a resolution to enter into a settlement agreement resolving the pending litigation and allowing the developer to proceed with construction of the project. In November 2025, construction of the project was completed, and the facility began operating with a total of 54 wind turbines and a generating capacity of 214 MW.

description: The viability of MidAmerican Energy’s plans to construct the 90-turbine Siouxland Wind Farm is in doubt due to Woodbury County’s adoption of an ordinance in August 2022 that increased the setback distance from wind turbines to occupied residences from 1,250 feet to 2,500 feet.
long_description: The viability of MidAmerican Energy’s plans to construct the 90-turbine Siouxland Wind Farm is in doubt due to Woodbury County’s adoption of an ordinance in August 2022 that increased the setback distance from wind turbines to occupied residences from 1,250 feet to 2,500 feet. As described above, the ordinance reduced the buildable acres in the county from 177 to 1.7. Opponents of the project cited noise and visual impacts, and over 700 residents signed a petition to increase the setback distance. Opponents of the project are seeking further changes to the ordinances regulating wind turbines, up to and including a ban on wind farms, and have stated that “[MidAmerican] just need[s] to pack up and go somewhere else where it’s more suitable.” MidAmerican is still looking to move forward with this project despite heavy resistance and ordinance changes.

description: The proposed Lava Ridge Wind Energy Project would be the largest wind farm in Idaho, with 400 turbines up to 740 feet tall producing 1,000 MW of electricity on federal land.
county: Jerome County; Lincoln County; Minidoka County
long_description: The proposed Lava Ridge Wind Energy Project would be the largest wind farm in Idaho, with 400 turbines up to 740 feet tall producing 1,000 MW of electricity on federal land. However, it has encountered opposition due to its size and proximity to the Minidoka National Historic Site where 13,000 Japanese Americans were imprisoned during the 1940s. In May 2022, the National Trust for Historic Preservation named the Minidoka National Historic Site as one of the eleven most endangered historic places in the country due to the proposed wind farm, which would be visible from the visitor center. In July and August 2022, all three counties in which the project would be located passed resolutions against it. On January 20, 2023, BLM released a draft environmental impact statement in which BLM stated that its two preferred alternatives would consist of a reduced number of turbines (269 or 378 turbines rather than the 400 turbines the developer is seeking to construct), due to concerns raised in the review process. In March 2023, the Idaho House and Idaho Senate each adopted unanimous resolutions opposing the project. In April 2023, the commissioners of the following Idaho counties signed a joint resolution against the project: Cassia, Gooding, Jerome, Lincoln, Minidoka, Washington, and Twin Falls. In August 2023, BLM announced that the lands for the proposed project would be kept open for two more years to allow BLM time to determine if it will authorize the project. In October 2023, an Idaho Congressman introduced a bill to prevent the Secretary of Interior from approving a wind or solar project over state legislative disapproval, which would have the effect of blocking the Lava Ridge project. In December 2024, the Bureau of Land Management issued a record of decision approving the project. [Note: In a presidential memorandum issued on January 20, 2025, President Trump imposed a stop-work order on the project, effectively preventing the project from moving forward.]
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

long_description: In January 2025, SunCode LLC proposed the 25.2-MW Belvidere Solar project to be located on approximately 120 acres in Caledonia Township. In May 2025, the Boone County Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) recommended approval of a special use permit for the project, subject to 19 conditions. In July 2025, the Boone County Administration Committee held a public meeting at which several local residents raised concerns over the project’s impact on property value, loss of agricultural land, and visual impacts. The Committee recommended denial of the proposal and submitted it to the Boone County Board for a final decision. On July 31, 2025, the Board, in an 8-2 vote, approved the special use permit in accordance with the ZBA recommendation. description: In 2015, Clean Line Energy proposed a project to build 207 miles of a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power line between the Mississippi River and Indiana border to transmit clean energy.
county: Christian County; Clark County; Cumberland County; Greene County; Macoupin County; Montgomery County; Pike County; Scott County; Shelby County
long_description: In 2015, Clean Line Energy proposed a project to build 207 miles of a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power line between the Mississippi River and Indiana border to transmit clean energy. The Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) first approved it in 2015. Landowner and agriculture groups called Concerned Citizens and Property Owners, Illinois Agricultural Association, and Landowners Alliance of Central Illinois challenged the approval in state court, and, in 2018, an Illinois appellate court overturned the approval on the grounds that regulators improperly allowed the company to use an expedited review process. The project was eventually taken over in 2020 by Invenergy, but the previous court order still prevented the project from going forward. In 2022, Gov. J.B. Pritzker signed the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which enabled construction to proceed despite the court’s ruling. The ICC approved the project for the second time in March 2023, allowing Invenergy to start building the HVDC power line. In August 2023, an Illinois appellate court enacted a stay on implementation of the March 2023 order to decide the project’s constitutionality. In September 2023, the court lifted the stay allowing the developer to continue with planning while the appeal moves forward. In August 2024, the Illinois appellate court reversed the ICC’s March 2023 approval of the project, citing issues with the financing of the project. In November 2024, the state’s Supreme Court granted leave to hear the appeal of the appellate court’s ruling. On July 23, 2025 the U.S. Department of Energy announced the cancellation of a $4.9 billion conditional federal loan guarantee for phase one of the project from Ford County, Kansas to Callaway County, Missouri. In January 2026, the Illinois Supreme Court decided the pending appeal and ruled in favor of the developer, allowing the company to move forward with construction of the project.

description: In 2026, SB Energy proposed the Shawnee Energy Project, a solar energy facility, to be located on private land spanning Massac and Johnson Counties.
long_description: In 2026, SB Energy proposed the Shawnee Energy Project, a solar energy facility, to be located on private land spanning Massac and Johnson Counties. The Johnson County Commission granted a special use permit for that County’s portion of the project, which comprises approximately 200 MW of solar generation on 1,100 acres. In February 2026, the developer submitted an application for the special use permit to the Massac County Commission for the remaining portion of the project. On February 24, 2026, the developer hosted a public meeting at the Metropolis Elks Lodge, which was attended by the Massac County Commissioners and approximately 75 local residents. During the meeting, residents opposed to the project questioned why the meeting was not held as a formal public hearing, with a question-and-answer session. The county commissioners rescheduled the meeting. In April 2026, the Massac County Commission held a public hearing on the project at the county courthouse. Opponents of the project raised concerns about loss of farmland, excess of stormwater runoff, and questioned the lifespan of the project and decommissioning plans. The developer stated that the footprint of the Massac County portion of the project had been reduced to 650 acres and its capacity reduced from 300 MW to 150 MW. The project is estimated to produce a total of $20 million of property taxes for Massac County over the next 25 to 35 years and create 450 jobs during construction. As of June 2026, the Massac County Commission was yet to make a decision on whether to approve the project.

description: In 2023, Evergy proposed the Kansas Sky Energy Center Solar Project, a 159-MW solar farm to be developed on approximately 1,103 acres in Grant Township near Lawrence, Kansas.
long_description: In 2023, Evergy proposed the Kansas Sky Energy Center Solar Project, a 159-MW solar farm to be developed on approximately 1,103 acres in Grant Township near Lawrence, Kansas. The project developer sought a conditional use permit from the Douglas County Planning Commission. The Commission received approximately 50 comments on the project, 30 of which expressed opposition to it. Voices against the project focused on the need to preserve agricultural land. In December 2023, the Douglas County Planning Commission’s review ended in a split 4-4 vote on the permit application. In April 2024, the Commission unanimously voted to approve the conditional use permit. In May 2024, a group of opponents of the project brought a lawsuit in the Douglas County District Court alleging that the approval of the permit conflicts with the County’s comprehensive plan and solar regulations. In December 2024, the District Court Judge issued an injunction preventing any construction on the project until the litigation is resolved. In October 2025, the Douglas County Commissioners voted unanimously to approve five temporary business use permits (TBUs) allowing the developer to conduct environmental testing for the project subject to a number of conditions while the litigation remains pending.

In June 2020, the parties voluntarily stipulated to dismissal, and the project entered commercial operation in 2021.

In July 2021, the developer filed a lawsuit alleging that the protest petitions were invalid, but in May 2020, the court ruled against the developer. In August 2022, the state appellate court upheld the decision that the protest petitions were legally sufficient to force a unanimous decision.

long_description: In June 2024, after more than 2.5 hours of comments at a public meeting, the St. James Parish Council denied by 4-3 vote a land use permit for St. James Solar, a 2,200-acre, 360-MW solar farm proposed by D.E. The project, however, would have required a special exception from the agricultural and residential land use designations in the land use plan, which prohibit solar farms, and that exception was denied. DESRI’s original plan for a 3,500-acre version of the project had prompted the Council to enact a moratorium and a new ordinance on solar farms in 2022.

long_description: In 2011, the Town of Amherst selected SunEdison to build a 2.4-MW solar array on a capped town landfill. In response, citizens filed a lawsuit against town officials for allegedly violating an agreement with the state that the landfill site must be used for recreational purposes. The lawsuit became moot in February 2012, when the state legislature passed a bill allowing all capped municipal landfills to serve as sites for solar projects. In April 2012, plaintiffs amended the lawsuit to include potential impacts to habitat of the grasshopper sparrow, which is protected under the Massachusetts Endangered Species Act. The lawsuit was dismissed without prejudice in December 2015. However, in July 2016 town officials terminated their contract with SunEdison after learning from the Massachusetts Division of Fisheries and Wildlife that the landfill solar project would likely impact habitat of the grasshopper sparrow.

long_description: In 2019, PureSky Energy proposed the Cape Cod Solar project on approximately 83 acres (out of over 200 acres) of a former country club golf course in the Town of Falmouth. The project consists of three solar facilities with battery energy storage systems (BESS) and has a total capacity of up to 13.5 MW. A Change.org petition garnered over 3,500 signatures to preserve the nearly 100-year-old golf course. Other opponents have expressed a preference for the development of housing, rather than the solar facility, on the land. In September 2025, the Cape Cod Commission, in a 14-1 vote, approved the conversion of the golf course. In November 2025, the Town approved the site conversion plans which include donating approximately 137 acres to the town to be protected as permanent open space. The solar project will now go before the Falmouth Planning Board for site plan review.

description: Two turbines known as Falmouth Wind 1 and 2, which were installed in 2010 and 2013, faced opposition from neighbors based in part on concerns about noise and health impacts.
long_description: Two turbines known as Falmouth Wind 1 and 2, which were installed in 2010 and 2013, faced opposition from neighbors based in part on concerns about noise and health impacts. In March 2013, two residents of the Town of Falmouth filed a complaint with the Falmouth Building Commissioner alleging that two wind turbines were a nuisance. The Building Commissioner denied the request to compel the Town to shut the turbines down. However, in December 2013, after holding a public meeting, the Falmouth Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) found that the turbines were a nuisance and overturned the denial. In 2014, the Town of Falmouth, as owner and operator of the turbines, filed a lawsuit in state court against the ZBA, alleging that the ZBA’s decision to shut down the turbines was arbitrary and capricious. The court sided with the ZBA, finding that the wind turbines posed a nuisance and ordering that the turbines be permanently stopped. By October 2022, the Town had demolished the two wind turbines.

project_name: New England Wind 2, formerly known as Commonwealth Wind Project and Park City Wind
description: In 2017, Avangrid began the development of two offshore wind farms south of Martha’s Vineyard – Commonwealth Wind (1,200-MW) and Park City Wind (800-MW).
long_description: In 2017, Avangrid began the development of two offshore wind farms south of Martha’s Vineyard – Commonwealth Wind (1,200-MW) and Park City Wind (800-MW). In April 2023, the developer filed a lawsuit against the Edgartown Conservation Commission after the town denied the company’s request to install subsurface transmission cables in town waters (see separate entry for New England Wind 1). Avangrid received a favorable ruling from the court, and in September 2023, the Commission rescinded its denial of the request. At a November 2023 Town public meeting concerning offshore wind, many Barnstable residents opposed plans to bring the cable installation, expressing concerns about disruption to public beaches and roads and impacts from electromagnetic fields. The citizen group Save Greater Dowses Beach formed in opposition to Avangrid’s plans to install the cables. In December 2023, the state Energy Facilities Siting Board voted to permit the landing of underground cables for the projects at Craigville Beach in Barnstable. In April 2024, the Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) reviewed and approved the projects, which were combined and rebranded as New England Wind 2. In May 2025, the group ACK for Whales filed a lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Columbia challenging the project alleging that the BOEM approval process violated several federal environmental laws, including the Marine Mammal Protection Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. In September 2025, the Department of Interior filed a motion indicating that it is reconsidering its 2024 permit approval for the project. The litigation remains pending.

description: In September 2021, the Northfield Planning Board approved a proposal by BlueWave Solar for a solar energy project that would cover 76 acres on three noncontiguous tracts.
long_description: In September 2021, the Northfield Planning Board approved a proposal by BlueWave Solar for a solar energy project that would cover 76 acres on three noncontiguous tracts. In November 2022, an abutter and an organization called “RESTORE: The North Woods” filed an appeal to contest the issuance of permits. The complaint alleged that the project would cause the abutter to “suffer a loss of the rural and agricultural values and aesthetic of the scenic country setting” and harm “prime farmland.” In April 2023, a Franklin County Superior Court judge ruled that the plaintiffs had standing to pursue their claim, allowing the case to proceed to trial. However, the following September, the parties agreed to dismiss the appeal, allowing the project to move forward.

description: In 2021, Sunpin Energy proposed the 4.3-MW Petersham Solar project to be located on approximately 14 acres in Petersham, Worcester County.
long_description: In 2021, Sunpin Energy proposed the 4.3-MW Petersham Solar project to be located on approximately 14 acres in Petersham, Worcester County. In November 2021, after four public meetings, the Petersham Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) voted 2-1 to approve the developer’s application for a special use permit for the project. However, as a unanimous vote was required, the permit was not issued. The dissenting board member and local residents opposing the project, expressed concern that it would require the cross-cutting of forest in a 14-acre parcel and harm the character of the community. In December 2021, the developer challenged the ZBA’s decision in the Massachusetts Land Court. In August 2023, the Land Court ruled that the ZBA had acted within their authority and the denial was reasonable based on public safety, health, and welfare. The developer subsequently challenged the Land Court’s ruling in the Massachusetts Appeals Court. In July 2025, the Appeals Court reversed, holding that the proposed use was allowed with a special permit, and that the ZBA had exceeded their discretion in denying the permit. The matter is currently on appeal by the ZBA before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court.

project_name: SouthCoast Wind, f/k/a Mayflower Wind, Falmouth Connection
description: SouthCoast Wind is a proposed 2,400-MW offshore project that would be located 30 miles south of Martha’s Vineyard and 20 miles south of Nantucket.
long_description: SouthCoast Wind is a proposed 2,400-MW offshore project that would be located 30 miles south of Martha’s Vineyard and 20 miles south of Nantucket. The developer is seeking to connect the project to the grid at two separate sites in Somerset and Falmouth, Massachusetts. The potential landing site in Falmouth, however, has faced local opposition. On December 19, 2022, the Select Board of the Town of Falmouth denied the developer’s request for access to town property to conduct soil testing for suitability of a landing site. In August 2023, SouthCoast Wind petitioned to terminate the project’s power purchase agreements. SouthCoast received new power purchase agreements with Massachusetts and Rhode Island in September 2024. In October 2024, the project received approval from Massachusetts’ Energy Facilities Siting Board for the project’s transmission facilities, along with approvals from the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection and Massachusetts Office of Coastal Zone Management. On October 30, 2024, the town of Nantucket’s special legal counsel, Cultural Heritage Partners, submitted a letter to BOEM raising concerns about mitigation measures and emergency response plans for blade failures. [Note: In February 2025, the developer announced that the project could be delayed until 2029 due to uncertainty related to federal policy.]

description: In 2025, Lodestar Energy proposed the 3.5-MW Van Deusenville Solar Project to be located on a 12-acre parcel of land zoned as a residential district in the Town of Great Barrington.
long_description: In 2025, Lodestar Energy proposed the 3.5-MW Van Deusenville Solar Project to be located on a 12-acre parcel of land zoned as a residential district in the Town of Great Barrington. In November 2025, following a public hearing, the Great Barrington Selectboard voted unanimously to recommend denial of the special permit for the project. Opponents of the project raised concerns over the potential for noise and the impact on the residential character of the neighborhood, and asserted that the project would be better suited for a commercial zone. Supporters of the project asserted the potential for an increase in tax revenues. The project will next be considered by the Planning Board for a final decision on the permit application.

description: In 2017, Avangrid Renewables proposed a 62-turbine, 800-MW offshore wind project located more than 15 miles of Martha’s Vineyard.
long_description: In 2017, Avangrid Renewables proposed a 62-turbine, 800-MW offshore wind project located more than 15 miles of Martha’s Vineyard. The project has faced opposition from fishing industry groups, a solar developer, and a local citizen group called Nantucket Residents Against Turbines (ACKRATS). In 2021 and 2022, these groups filed four separate lawsuits against the project in federal court. All four lawsuits alleged insufficient consideration of potential impacts to right whales, among other claims. The cases include claims under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA), Clean Water Act (CWA), Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and the Merchant Marine Act of 1920. Between May and October 2023, the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts decided all four cases in favor of Vineyard Wind and the federal government. All four cases were appealed to the First Circuit. In April 2024, the First Circuit affirmed the lower court’s decision in two of the cases: Nantucket Residents Against Turbines v. U.S. Bureau of Energy Management, and Melone v. Coit. In December 2024, the First Circuit affirmed dismissal of two related lawsuits by Responsible Offshore Development Alliance (RODA) and Seafreeze Shoreside. In September 2024, Nantucket Residents Against Turbines filed a petition for certiorari in the U.S. Supreme Court. In January 2025, the certiorari petition was denied. RODA and Seafreeze subsequently filed petitions for certiorari, but those petitions were also denied in May 2025. On December 22, 2025, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) issued a stop-work order to halt construction of the project for reasons of national security. In January 2026, the developer filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts to enjoin BOEM’s stop-work order. In late January 2026, the federal district judge granted the plaintiff’s request for a preliminary injunction and allowed construction of the project to resume.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: In 2025, Halo Betterton, LLC proposed the 5-MW Betterton Halo Solar project to be located on approximately 30 acres of land in the Town of Betterton.
long_description: In 2025, Halo Betterton, LLC proposed the 5-MW Betterton Halo Solar project to be located on approximately 30 acres of land in the Town of Betterton. In April 2025, the developer applied for the required Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) from the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC). In May 2025, the Maryland Department of Natural Resources recommended that the application be deemed administratively complete. In September 2025, the PSC held a public hearing on the project at which town officials expressed their opposition to it, citing concerns about potential impacts to the town’s residential character and public safety risks because the project site would block their designated helicopter landing zone. Nearly two dozen opponents at that hearing also raised concerns over historical preservation, public safety, and impacts on property values. In November 2025, a town community meeting was held at which over 50 local residents and representatives of regional preservation groups, including the Kent Conservation and Preservation Alliance, objected to the project, primarily on the grounds that the proposed project site is restricted to residential use. description: The Maryland Offshore Wind Project, proposed by US Wind, has the potential to generate up to 2,200 MW.
long_description: The Maryland Offshore Wind Project, proposed by US Wind, has the potential to generate up to 2,200 MW. The project has encountered opposition from the Ocean City government and the tourism industry due to concerns that visual impacts will harm business. In February 2018, the Ocean City Mayor and Council unanimously approved a resolution against any wind project being sited within 30 miles of the city. The City officials proposed a similar bill in the General Assembly that would have required siting at least 26 miles off the coast, but the Maryland House of Delegates rejected the proposed legislation. In September 2021, after the developer applied for an expansion of the project size, several local elected officials and business leaders expressed concern about turbines ruining beachfront views, jeopardizing tourism, and negatively impacting real estate values and the local economy. In November 2023, Worcester County Commissioners sent a letter to the Army Corps of Engineers urging the Corps to deny a permit for US Wind. In October 2024, Ocean City and other plaintiffs, including Worcester County, various community associations, and the Ocean City Marlin Club, filed a lawsuit in federal court, alleging that the federal government’s approval of the project violated the Administrative Procedure Act, National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, Marine Mammal Protection Act, Migratory Bird Treaty Act, Coastal Zone Management Act, Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, and National Historic Preservation Act. In December 2024, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management issued its final approval of the project. In January 2025, the Army Corps issued the permit for the project. In July 2025, the federal court ruled on the motions to dismiss the case by the federal defendants and the developer intervenor. While the court dismissed several of the claims, it allowed the claims under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act to proceed, and reserved judgment on the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and the National Environmental Policy Act claims. In September 2025, the Department of Interior filed a motion indicating that it planned to withdraw its approval for the project and alleging that the approval process did not address potential impacts on other offshore uses, such as fishing. The litigation remains pending.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: The Aroostook Renewable Gateway Project is a 150-mile, 1,200-MW transmission corridor designed to transmit energy from the proposed 170-turbine King Pine Wind Farm in Aroostook County to consumers in southern Maine and Massachusetts.

long_description: The Aroostook Renewable Gateway Project is a 150-mile, 1,200-MW transmission corridor designed to transmit energy from the proposed 170-turbine King Pine Wind Farm in Aroostook County to consumers in southern Maine and Massachusetts. LS Power was initially developing the project. In June 2023, Maine adopted a bill approving the project, but the project has been slowed by local opposition and moratoria. Maine residents opposing the project have raised concerns about impacts to property and sightlines, formed a citizen group called Preserve Rural Maine, and obtained legal counsel. In August 2023, in response to this project, the town of Albion imposed a 6-month moratorium on utility lines and corridors, with residents expressing concerns that the project would disrupt farmland and that the project’s electromagnetic fields would disorient bees. Also, in response to the project, in September 2023, the Town of Palermo adopted a transmission line moratorium. In November 2023, the Town of Unity adopted a 180-day moratorium on high-voltage power lines. In December 2023, LS Power announced that it could no longer proceed with the project at the agreed-upon price. In response, the Maine Public Utilities Commission announced that it was terminating its agreement with LS Power and delaying development until it could find another developer for the project. However, in October 2024, the Department of Energy announced a $425 million capacity contract with Avangrid to restart conversations with the Maine PUC on continuing the transmission project. In November 2024, the Town of China’s select board passed a 180-day High-Impact Electric Transmission Line Moratorium Ordinance in response to the project.

description: In 2012, the organization Friends of Maine Mountains (“Friends”) filed an appeal with the Maine Supreme Judicial Court challenging the state Board of Environmental Protection (BEP)’s February 18, 2012 final order approving the 34-MW Saddleback Ridge Wind Project.
long_description: In 2012, the organization Friends of Maine Mountains (“Friends”) filed an appeal with the Maine Supreme Judicial Court challenging the state Board of Environmental Protection (BEP)’s February 18, 2012 final order approving the 34-MW Saddleback Ridge Wind Project. The BEP’s order affirmed the state Department of Environmental Protection (DEP)’s approval of the project. Friends alleged that BEP misapplied the nighttime sound limits and argued that certain provisions of the Maine Wind Energy Act were unconstitutional. In March 2013, the court unanimously vacated the BEP’s decision and remanded for further administrative proceedings. The court found that BEP abused its discretion by allowing 45 dBA of noise during the nighttime after having adopted a nighttime limit of 42 dBA. The court, however, found no merit in Friends’ constitutional challenges to the Maine Wind Energy Act.

description: RWE Clean Energy proposed a 200-MW solar farm, called 45th Parallel Solar, to be developed on approximately 1,000 acres of private land in Hayes Township.
long_description: RWE Clean Energy proposed a 200-MW solar farm, called 45th Parallel Solar, to be developed on approximately 1,000 acres of private land in Hayes Township. In February 2025, the Otsego County Planning Commission, in a 7-1 vote, approved a special use permit for the project. The developer had submitted a separate proposal to lease additional public land for the project. In May 2025, the Michigan Department of Natural Resources rejected the leasing proposal following mass public criticism from both lawmakers and environmental organizations, citing concerns over deforestation and a lack of transparency. The development of the project continues on the proposed 1,000 acres of private land and commercial operations are estimated to begin in 2027.

description: Ranger Power has proposed to construct a 170-MW solar facility called Birch Valley Solar on approximately 1,500 acres of farmland in Arbela Township.
long_description: Ranger Power has proposed to construct a 170-MW solar facility called Birch Valley Solar on approximately 1,500 acres of farmland in Arbela Township. If completed, the project would net $340,000 annually for the township’s fire, infrastructure, or safety expenses. The proposal also includes a host community agreement requiring the developer to pay the township $2,000 per MW of installed capacity. Despite the anticipated benefits, the project is facing local opposition. Opponents have raised concerns of encroachment on prime farmland and the fact that the project’s scale would exceed the local zoning ordinance’s cap on utility-scale solar development of 4% of total township acreage. In July 2025, the developer submitted an application for a special land use permit. If the Arbela Township Board of Trustees denies the permit, the developer may seek project approval from the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) under the Public Act 233 of 2023, which allows the PSC to preempt certain  local government decisions.

long_description: In April 2022, the Fulton Township Board officially rejected a recommendation from the Fulton Planning Commission to move forward with the Heartland Wind project. The unanimous vote (4-0) came after a heated four-hour-long town hall meeting. The developer, Invenergy, had intended to construct 12 turbines in Fulton and sued the Township after the Board’s decision, but a judge dismissed the suit. Invenergy continued to move forward with the project despite the Board’s decision, as it had received approval from the five other affected townships. Construction on the wind farm began in April 2023. The 201-MW, 72-turbine project was operational as of January 2024, with capacity to power roughly 80,000 homes.

long_description: In 2025, DTE Energy proposed the Iosco Solar project to be located on approximately 1,800 acres of land spanning two districts zoned as agricultural land in Iosco Township. description: In April 2013, Mason County residents, supported by Citizens Alliance for Responsible Renewable Energy, filed a lawsuit in Mason County Circuit Court, challenging the Mason County Planning Commission’s approval of Consumers Energy’s 100-MW Lake Winds Energy Park and seeking an injunction to stop the project’s operations.
long_description: In April 2013, Mason County residents, supported by Citizens Alliance for Responsible Renewable Energy, filed a lawsuit in Mason County Circuit Court, challenging the Mason County Planning Commission’s approval of Consumers Energy’s 100-MW Lake Winds Energy Park and seeking an injunction to stop the project’s operations. The project, which consists of 56 turbines, had been operational since November 2012. The plaintiffs alleged that noise, vibrations, and flickering light were causing physical harm as well as economic losses. The developer had received 128 complaints within the first year of operation and had faced opposition during construction. In September 2013, the Mason County Planning Commission determined that the wind farm violated the agreed-upon noise standards and ordered Consumers Energy to bring the facility into compliance. In late 2014, the developer reached a confidential settlement that resolved the pending lawsuit.

description: In March 2016, several Sanilac County townships acted to delay or prevent the siting of the 68-turbine, 150-MW Michigan Wind 3 project being developed by Exelon.
long_description: In March 2016, several Sanilac County townships acted to delay or prevent the siting of the 68-turbine, 150-MW Michigan Wind 3 project being developed by Exelon. Marion Township approved a moratorium on wind energy development, which was expected to push the project back at least six months, though the moratorium was later amended to apply only to future permit applications. Marion Township residents stated that they were preparing for legal action if the project was ultimately approved. A Bridgehampton Township council member moved for a wind moratorium at the same time. This proposed moratorium was eventually rejected. Exelon also sued Bridgehampton Township for tabling a public hearing on Exelon’s application for a special land use permit, but a Sanilac County judge ruled against Exelon in May 2016. Bridgehampton then adopted a six-month moratorium on new wind development in November 2016 under a new board supervisor. The project does not appear to have been built.

description: In 2017, Invenergy proposed the 150-MW Mustang Mile Solar project to be located on approximately 2,777 acres in Macon Township.
long_description: In 2017, Invenergy proposed the 150-MW Mustang Mile Solar project to be located on approximately 2,777 acres in Macon Township. From 2018 to 2020, the township adopted amendments to its solar ordinance to allow large-scale solar facilities as a special land use. However, in 2021, the Planning Commission recommended denial of a permit for the Mustang Mile Solar project on the basis that it did not meet the required standards for a special land use. The Township Board, in a 3-2 vote, approved issuance of a special use permit for the project, despite the Commission’s findings and recommendation to deny it. In 2021, local opponents of the project filed a lawsuit in the Lenawee Circuit Court challenging the Board’s issuance of the permit. The circuit court affirmed the Board’s decision; in its ruling, the court erroneously stated that the Commission had recommended approval of the permit. The opponents appealed the circuit court’s decision to the Michigan Court of Appeals. In October 2025, the court of appeals vacated the circuit court’s decision reasoning that the lower court’s decision was an error unsupported by the record. The matter was remanded to the Board for further proceedings.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: In June 2019, Pegasus Wind applied for zoning variances to construct 33 wind turbines near a local airport.
long_description: In June 2019, Pegasus Wind applied for zoning variances to construct 33 wind turbines near a local airport. The Tuscola Airport Zoning Board of Appeals (AZBA) denied the applications for variances, citing concerns about air traffic safety. The developer appealed the denials to the Tuscola Circuit Court, which reversed the AZBA’s decision. In October 2019, Pegasus Wind submitted applications for 8 additional variances, which the AZBA again denied. Pegasus Wind appealed the denial to the Tuscola Circuit Court, which affirmed the denial. In 2022, the Michigan Court of Appeals reversed the Circuit Court’s decision, finding that denial was improper. However, in April 2024, the Michigan Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals’ decision, allowing the AZBA’s denial of the variances to stand.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv
