description: In January 2024, Vista Sands Solar, LLC (Vista Sands), an affiliate of Doral Renewables, proposed Vista Sands Solar, a 1,300-MW solar farm with a 300-MW battery energy storage system which would be the largest solar farm in the state.
long_description: In January 2024, Vista Sands Solar, LLC (Vista Sands), an affiliate of Doral Renewables, proposed Vista Sands Solar, a 1,300-MW solar farm with a 300-MW battery energy storage system which would be the largest solar farm in the state. The project would be located on approximately 9,500 acres of privately-owned agricultural land in the Village of Plover and towns of Grant, Plover and Buena Vista. An alliance of opponents including hunters, birdwatchers and public land advocates opposed the project and raised concerns about impacts to the greater prairie-chicken population, a threatened species. The Wisconsin Wildlife Federation intervened in the regulatory approval process asking the Public Service Commission (PSC) to reduce the project size by 20 to 30 percent to better protect the birds’ habitats. In July 2024 the PSC and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources issued a joint final Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) that recommended scaling back the plans by removing 10 of the proposed areas for solar arrays. The agencies had received over 400 comments on their draft EIS. In December 2024, after reviewing the developer’s detailed report of the public health, ecosystem and economic benefits of the project, the PSC unanimously approved the scaled down version of the project and described it as one of the most valuable for the state. The developer agreed to restore up to 7,900 acres of agricultural land in the vicinity of the wildlife area, to seed the area under development with a beneficial wildflower mix, and not to construct within 500 feet of important habitat for the great prairie chicken. Construction is expected to begin in late 2025 and the project is expected to produce enough electricity to power about 200,000 homes.

description: In 2024, Ranger Power proposed the 180-MW Whitewater Solar project to be located on approximately 2,800 acres of farmland.
long_description: In 2024, Ranger Power proposed the 180-MW Whitewater Solar project to be located on approximately 2,800 acres of farmland. The project site includes land within the City of Whitewater and Town of Cold Spring in Jefferson County, and the Towns of Whitewater and LaGrange in Walworth County. Opponents of the project intervened in the permitting process before the Wisconsin Public Service Commission (PSC) and raised several objections, including the loss of farmland, impacts to the tourist and rural character of the community, and impacts to the nearby Kettle Moraine State Forest. In September 2025, the Wisconsin PSC unanimously approved the project. The opponents requested a second hearing before the Wisconsin PSC. In November 2025, the Wisconsin PSC issued its final decision, affirming its approval finding that the project is in the public interest, it will not have undue adverse impacts on environmental values, and it does not unreasonably interfere with the orderly use of land. The opponents launched an online campaign to raise funds for legal fees to support an appeal challenging the PSC’s decision.

description: The Beech Ridge Wind Farm, a 100-MW wind project in Greenbrier County, was met with local opposition when it was proposed in 2005.
long_description: The Beech Ridge Wind Farm, a 100-MW wind project in Greenbrier County, was met with local opposition when it was proposed in 2005. Opponents including the Animal Welfare Institute and Mountain Communities for Responsible Energy challenged the project before the PSC, and then in federal court. During the pendency of the federal lawsuit, the developer agreed to continue construction on only 40 out of the planned 124 turbines until a decision on the merits. In 2009, a federal district court found flaws in analysis of impacts on the endangered Indiana bat and imposed severe restrictions on the project. The court allowed the developer to complete the 40 turbines under construction but enjoined the operation of those wind turbines at all times except winter, unless the parties could agree otherwise. The project was completed in 2010 with the construction of 67 turbines.

long_description: In 2025, Enel North America proposed the 100-MW Brandonville Solar project to be located on approximately 1,000 acres between Glade Run and Big Sandy Creek, about one mile north of Brandonville. Opponents of the project, including State Delegate George Street, raised concerns about loss of farmland and impacts on property values and wildlife, and noted that, according to the Interconnection Field Study, the actual output of the solar farm is estimated to be about 50 percent less than proposed. In February 2026, the PSC concluded that the project is not contrary to the public interest given its positive economic impact on Preston County and the state of West Virginia, and thus granted the siting certificate. description: In 2022, Focus Clean Energy proposed the “Pronghorn H2” project, comprising a roughly 300 MW wind farm and 280 MW solar farm, to power a hydrogen production facility.
long_description: In 2022, Focus Clean Energy proposed the “Pronghorn H2” project, comprising a roughly 300 MW wind farm and 280 MW solar farm, to power a hydrogen production facility. The project is to be located on public and private lands spanning a total of approximately 40,000 acres near Glenrock. The project has faced strong opposition from local ranchers, landowners, and a group called “Taxpayers Against Pronghorn H2 Project.” The opponents have raised concerns over public safety, water use, viewshed impacts, impacts on wildlife migration, and interference with private property rights. In April 2025, the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners, in a 4-1 vote, approved a lease for the project. With the same vote, the Board also approved a lease for another project by the same developers in neighboring Niobrara County (see Sidewinder Wind). In July 2025, a local rancher filed a lawsuit in the district court challenging the state approval of the Pronghorn project. In December 2025, the district court ruled that the Board had violated its own rules by approving the lease for the project. In January 2026, the developer revised the project proposal, reducing its size to 30% of the initial footprint and indicating that it would move forward with only the wind and solar facilities and not the hydrogen production component of the project. In February 2026, the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners, in a 3-2 vote, rescinded the land lease for the project. Chuck Gray, Wyoming Secretary of State and the only member of the Board of Land Commissioners to initially vote against the proposals, released a statement after the vote celebrating the cancellation of “woke wind leases.”
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: The Rail Tie Wind Project, a 26,000-acre, 504-MW wind farm proposed by ConnectGen (which was acquired by Repsol in March 2024), has experienced delays after becoming embroiled in legal controversies.
long_description: The Rail Tie Wind Project, a 26,000-acre, 504-MW wind farm proposed by ConnectGen (which was acquired by Repsol in March 2024), has experienced delays after becoming embroiled in legal controversies. At a meeting in February 2020, residents urged the county planning and zoning commission to place a moratorium on wind development to block the project, citing concerns about the potential for aesthetic changes to the classic western landscape, effects on local wildlife, and the potential for groundwater contamination during the installation of turbine foundations. An attorney representing landowners opposed to the project also lobbied the county to impose aggressive setback requirements that would effectively block wind energy projects. However, neither the moratorium nor the setbacks were implemented. While the State Board of Land Commissioners initially denied the developer’s lease application on 4,800 acres of state land in November 2020, the Board reversed its decision and approved the lease in January 2021. The Albany County Board of Commissioners then granted final approval in July 2021. Local residents and businesses challenged the permit, and, in May 2022, the Albany County district court upheld the permit. Over 45 residents signed onto an appeal to the Wyoming Supreme Court, and the Wyoming Supreme Court affirmed, upholding the permit on April 18, 2023. In December 2023, the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality’s Industrial Siting Council approved the project, drawing a lawsuit. On December 23, 2024, the Albany County Conservancy and other plaintiffs filed a lawsuit in federal court to stop the project, alleging violations of the NEPA, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act. The project, if completed, is expected to produce $130 million in tax revenues
